subject: HEALTH
overview: Health 8 is a 25-minute, skills-based course: each day the child reads or discusses a short concept, then practices a skill (analyzing influences, accessing valid information, communicating, deciding, setting goals, advocating). Talk more than you lecture — most lessons work best as a conversation with the parent, followed by a short written product in the health journal. Preview Unit 3 (weeks 11–18, sexual health under the CA Healthy Youth Act) and the suicide, overdose and violence lessons before teaching; you may opt out of sexual health instruction (Ed. Code 51938) and use the alternative assignment. Keep the tone calm and factual, and remind the child often who their trusted adults are and that 988 (call or text) is available 24/7.

weeks.prep: Have the health journal ready. Find a KidsHealth for Teens article on resilience (search 'resilience' on kidshealth.org/en/teens) and preview it. Gather paper and markers for a support web.
misconceptions: Thinking resilient people never feel upset. Correct: resilience is recovering and adapting after difficulty, not avoiding painful feelings.
Believing resilience is a fixed trait you are born with. Correct: it is built through skills, relationships and practice — that is why protective factors matter.

days.guide: List grade 7 coping strategies together (deep breathing, exercise, talking to someone, journaling, time management, sleep). Have the child rate each 1–5 for how often they use it, then circle one to use more.

questions.q: Name three healthy ways to cope with stress.
questions.a: Any three: slow deep breathing, physical activity, talking to a trusted person, journaling, breaking a task into steps, getting enough sleep, spending time on a hobby or outdoors.

days.guide: Read the article together and stop at each skill it names. The child lists the 'bounce back' skills in the journal and puts a star next to one they already use.

questions.q: What is resilience?
questions.a: The ability to cope with, adapt to and recover from stress, setbacks or hard experiences.

questions.q: Give two resilience skills.
questions.a: Examples: problem solving, positive self-talk, asking for help, staying connected to others, managing emotions, keeping perspective, taking care of the body.

days.guide: Explain protective factors versus risk factors. The child draws themself in the center of a page and adds spokes for people, activities, places and personal strengths that support them.

questions.q: What is the difference between a protective factor and a risk factor?
questions.a: A protective factor lowers the chance of negative outcomes (e.g., a caring adult, a team, good coping skills); a risk factor raises it (e.g., isolation, substance use, ongoing stress).

days.guide: Model one rewrite ('I'm bad at math' → 'I'm not good at this yet; I'll try a new strategy'). The child rewrites five fixed-mindset statements; check that each adds 'yet,' effort, strategy or learning from mistakes.

questions.q: Rewrite 'I give up, I'll never get this' as a growth-mindset statement.
questions.a: Example: 'This is hard right now, but if I practice and try a different strategy or ask for help, I can improve.'

days.guide: The child writes a reflection of a real setback (lost game, bad grade, friendship problem), what they did and which protective factors from the web helped. Discuss it together.

questions.q: Why do protective factors matter when facing a setback?
questions.a: They give support and resources — people to talk to, skills and activities — that help you recover faster and cope in healthy ways.

weeks.assessment_key: Support web (4 pts each, total 8): includes at least 3 people, 2 activities/places and 2 personal strengths, all labeled. Reflection: 4 = names a specific setback, the action taken, at least two protective factors and explains how each helped; 3 = setback and one protective factor with some explanation; 2 = vague setback, factors listed without explanation; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find where the device shows screen time (iPhone: Settings > Screen Time; Android: Digital Wellbeing). Preview a Common Sense Education lesson on digital wellbeing. Have last year's PE sleep log or start a two-day sleep log now.
misconceptions: Thinking all screen time is equally harmful. Correct: what you do (creating, connecting vs. endless scrolling), when (before bed) and how you feel afterward matter most.
Believing 'the app is free.' Correct: the user's attention and data are the product; features are designed to keep people engaged longer.

days.guide: Show the child how to open the screen-time report by app. They log two days of minutes per app (or keep a paper log if no device) and note how they felt after each.

questions.q: Which category of app takes most of your time, and is that how you want to spend it?
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer names the app category with minutes and makes an honest judgment about whether it matches their priorities.

days.guide: Explain that feeds are ranked by algorithms that predict what keeps you watching. Pick one platform and list design features: infinite scroll, autoplay, notifications, streaks, likes, variable rewards.

questions.q: Name two design features that keep users scrolling and explain one.
questions.a: Examples: infinite scroll removes natural stopping points; autoplay starts the next video automatically; streaks pressure daily use; notifications pull you back; likes give unpredictable rewards like a slot machine.

days.guide: Look at filtered vs. unfiltered photos (many creators post side-by-sides). Discuss highlight reels: people post their best moments. The child finds two examples and writes how they might affect someone's self-image.

questions.q: Why can comparing yourself to social media posts lower self-esteem?
questions.a: Posts are edited, filtered and selected highlights, so you compare your everyday life to others' best moments, which is unrealistic.

days.guide: Line up screen-time minutes in the hour before bed with bedtime and hours of sleep. The child writes one pattern (e.g., more late screen use → later sleep).

questions.q: How do screens before bed affect sleep?
questions.a: Blue light can delay melatonin, and engaging content keeps the brain alert, so it takes longer to fall asleep and total sleep drops; teens need about 8–10 hours.

days.guide: Review SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound). The child writes a tech-balance goal; you check each letter and sign it.

questions.q: Is 'I'll use my phone less' a SMART goal? Fix it.
questions.a: No — it is not specific, measurable or time-bound. Example fix: 'For the next 4 weeks, I will put my phone outside my bedroom by 9:30 p.m. on school nights and track it on a chart.'

weeks.assessment_key: Screen-time analysis (4 pts): two days logged by app, totals calculated, one pattern identified, one feeling noted. SMART goal (4 pts): 1 pt each for specific action, measurable tracking, realistic amount, time frame; parent signature required. Proficient: goal connects to a pattern found in the analysis (e.g., late-night use and sleep).

weeks.prep: Print or bookmark NAMI or KidsHealth fact sheets on anxiety disorders, ADHD, depression and OCD. Draw a continuum line labeled Healthy – Reacting – Struggling – Unwell (or Thriving to Crisis).
misconceptions: Thinking mental illness means someone is weak or 'crazy.' Correct: mental illnesses are common health conditions involving the brain, and they are treatable.
Confusing normal sadness or nervousness with a disorder. Correct: a disorder involves symptoms that are intense, last a long time and interfere with daily life.

days.guide: Draw the continuum and explain that everyone moves along it. Give everyday examples (good week, stressed before a test, can't sleep for weeks) and have the child place each.

questions.q: Where would 'feeling nervous before a big game but performing fine' go on the continuum?
questions.a: Toward the healthy/reacting end — it is a normal, temporary stress response that does not interfere with functioning.

days.guide: The child picks one condition, reads a fact sheet and lists 3–4 symptoms and 2 treatments. Check facts against the source.

questions.q: Name one symptom and one treatment for depression.
questions.a: Symptoms: persistent sadness or emptiness for two weeks or more, loss of interest, sleep or appetite changes, trouble concentrating, hopelessness. Treatments: talk therapy (e.g., CBT), medication, support, exercise and sleep routines.

questions.q: How is an anxiety disorder different from ordinary worry?
questions.a: The worry or fear is excessive, hard to control, lasts months and interferes with school, sleep or relationships.

days.guide: Show examples of stigmatizing words ('psycho,' 'crazy,' 'she's so OCD'). Teach person-first language and have the child rewrite three phrases.

questions.q: Rewrite 'He's a schizophrenic' using person-first language.
questions.a: 'He is a person who has schizophrenia' or 'He lives with schizophrenia.'

days.guide: Explain each professional: school counselor (support, referrals), psychologist (therapy and testing, not usually medication), psychiatrist (medical doctor who can prescribe medication), licensed therapist. Discuss how to access: tell a parent, school counselor, doctor.

questions.q: Which professional can prescribe medication?
questions.a: A psychiatrist (a medical doctor); a primary-care doctor or psychiatric nurse practitioner can also prescribe. Psychologists generally do not.

days.guide: The child makes a one-page infographic with at least two facts, one myth corrected, person-first language and where to get help.

questions.q: What is stigma and why does it matter?
questions.a: Negative attitudes and stereotypes about people with mental illness; it makes people ashamed and less likely to seek help.

weeks.assessment_key: Infographic rubric (4 levels): 4 = at least two accurate facts with source, one myth corrected, person-first language throughout, help resources (988, counselor, doctor), clear design; 3 = accurate facts and resources, minor gaps; 2 = one fact, no myth or resources, some stigmatizing wording; 1 = inaccurate or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: this week covers suicide warning signs. Read 988lifeline.org 'Know the signs' first. Make myth/fact cards. Be ready to talk calmly; if your child discloses thoughts of suicide, stay with them, listen and call or text 988 or the child's doctor.
misconceptions: Believing asking 'Are you thinking about suicide?' plants the idea. Correct: research shows asking directly does not increase risk and often brings relief.
Thinking you should keep a friend's secret if they ask. Correct: safety comes before secrecy — always tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Read each card aloud; the child sorts it as myth or fact and explains. Include: asking does not plant the idea (fact); people who talk about suicide won't do it (myth); suicide is preventable (fact).

questions.q: True or false: People who talk about suicide are just seeking attention.
questions.a: False (myth). Talking about suicide is a warning sign and must be taken seriously.

questions.q: True or false: Asking someone directly about suicide can help.
questions.a: True. It shows you care and opens the door to getting help.

days.guide: Make three columns: verbal, behavioral, situational. Fill them together from 988lifeline.org.

questions.q: Give one example of each type of warning sign.
questions.a: Verbal: 'I wish I were dead,' 'No one would miss me.' Behavioral: giving away belongings, withdrawing, increased substance use, saying goodbye, searching for means. Situational: a recent loss, breakup, bullying, major failure or family crisis.

days.guide: Model Ask-Listen-Tell: 'Are you thinking about killing yourself?' / listen without judging / 'Let's tell ____ together.' Then switch roles so the child practices.

questions.q: What are the three steps, and what do you do if a friend asks you to keep it a secret?
questions.a: Ask directly, Listen without judgment, Tell a trusted adult right away. Do not keep it secret; say you care too much to keep it.

days.guide: Help the child save 988 (call or text) and the Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741) and write three trusted adults with phone numbers.

questions.q: How do you reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline?
questions.a: Call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org, 24/7. In immediate danger, call 911.

days.guide: The child completes a wallet card (warning signs on one side, Ask-Listen-Tell and contacts on the other). Close with an open conversation about feelings.

questions.q: If a friend posts 'I can't do this anymore, goodbye everyone' late at night, what should you do?
questions.a: Treat it as an emergency: contact the friend if safe, tell a parent or trusted adult immediately, and call 911 or 988 to get help.

weeks.assessment_key: Wallet card: 4 = at least 3 accurate warning signs across categories, Ask-Listen-Tell steps, 988 and Crisis Text Line (741741), 3 named trusted adults; 3 = minor omission; 2 = missing resources or steps; 1 = incomplete. Role-play: proficient if the child asks the question directly, listens without arguing, refuses secrecy and names who they will tell.

weeks.prep: Choose a picture book or article on grief (e.g., KidsHealth 'Death and Grief'). Be sensitive to any recent losses in the family; this week can bring up strong feelings.
misconceptions: Thinking grief follows five stages in order. Correct: grief is not linear — feelings come and go, overlap and return, especially on anniversaries.
Believing the best way to help is to say 'I know how you feel' or 'They're in a better place.' Correct: listen, acknowledge the loss and offer specific help.

days.guide: Brainstorm types of loss together and write one feeling each might bring (sadness, anger, confusion, relief, guilt).

questions.q: Name three types of loss other than death.
questions.a: Examples: moving, parents' divorce, a friendship ending, losing a pet, injury that ends a sport, a change of school.

days.guide: Read the article together. Draw a tangled 'scribble' line vs. a straight line to show grief is not linear. List physical (tiredness, appetite change) and emotional reactions.

questions.q: Name one physical and one emotional reaction to grief.
questions.a: Physical: fatigue, trouble sleeping, headaches, stomachaches, appetite changes. Emotional: sadness, anger, guilt, numbness, anxiety, relief.

days.guide: Make a T-chart: helpful vs. unhelpful things to say. Practice saying one helpful line aloud.

questions.q: Give one helpful and one unhelpful thing to say to a grieving friend.
questions.a: Helpful: 'I'm so sorry. I'm here if you want to talk,' 'Do you want company at lunch?' Unhelpful: 'At least…,' 'I know exactly how you feel,' 'You should be over it by now.'

days.guide: The child picks three healthy coping strategies and writes when and how they'd use each. Point out unhealthy coping (isolating, substances) to avoid.

questions.q: When should grief be shared with an adult or counselor?
questions.a: When it does not ease over time, interferes with sleep, school or eating, or includes hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm.

days.guide: The child writes a letter of support to a fictional friend, using phrases from the helpful list and offering specific help.

questions.q: What makes a support letter helpful?
questions.a: It acknowledges the loss, expresses care, avoids minimizing, offers specific help and reminds the friend they're not alone.

weeks.assessment_key: Support letter: 4 = names the loss, acknowledges feelings, no minimizing phrases, offers at least two specific forms of help, mentions a trusted adult or resource; 3 = caring and specific but missing one element; 2 = generic or includes an unhelpful phrase; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather poster paper or set up slide/video software. Write a 12–15 question unit test on weeks 1–5 (use the key below). Have the child's SMART tech goal from week 2.
misconceptions: Making a PSA that only lists facts. Correct: an effective PSA has one clear message, a target audience and a call to action (e.g., 'Text 988').
Thinking resources are only for emergencies. Correct: counselors and doctors help with everyday struggles too.

days.guide: The child chooses a message (help-seeking or anti-stigma), an audience (teens) and a call to action, and sketches the plan.

questions.q: What three things does a PSA plan need?
questions.a: A clear message, a target audience and a specific call to action (plus accurate facts).

days.guide: The child creates the PSA. Check facts and that wording is person-first.

questions.q: What call to action would fit a help-seeking PSA?
questions.a: Examples: 'Talk to a trusted adult,' 'Call or text 988,' 'Visit your school counselor.'

days.guide: The child shows the PSA to family members and asks two feedback questions (Was the message clear? Would it change what you do?).

questions.q: Why gather audience feedback?
questions.a: To see whether the message is clear and persuasive and to improve it.

days.guide: Compare the tech log to the SMART goal. The child writes whether they met it and one adjustment.

questions.q: If you missed your goal, what should you do?
questions.a: Analyze what got in the way and adjust the plan (smaller step, new strategy, accountability) rather than giving up.

days.guide: Give the unit test closed-book; review missed items together.

questions.q: Name two protective factors.
questions.a: Examples: a supportive family, a trusted adult, friends, a team or club, coping skills, a sense of purpose.

weeks.assessment_key: PSA: 4 = accurate, one clear message, audience-appropriate, person-first, includes call to action and resource. Unit test key (sample items): 1) resilience = ability to adapt and recover from adversity 2) protective factor example: caring adult 3) fixed vs growth mindset: belief abilities can't vs can grow with effort 4) feeds use algorithms to maximize engagement 5) mental illness is common and treatable 6) psychiatrist can prescribe medication 7) person-first: 'person with depression' 8) asking about suicide does NOT plant the idea 9) warning signs: talking about death, giving away possessions, withdrawing 10) Ask-Listen-Tell 11) 988 call/text 24/7; Crisis Text Line text HOME to 741741 12) grief is not linear 13) helpful response: listen, offer specific help. 80%+ = proficient.

weeks.prep: Open myplate.gov 'MyPlate Plan' and preview the calculator with the child's age, sex, height, weight and activity. Collect 3–4 nutrition labels. Write a 10-question quiz from the key.
misconceptions: Thinking teens should eat as little as possible to stay healthy. Correct: adolescents need more energy and nutrients (especially calcium and iron) to fuel growth.
Believing all calories are the same nutritionally. Correct: energy balance is about calories, but nutrient density determines what the body gets for those calories.

days.guide: Explain energy in (food) vs. energy out (growth, basal metabolism, activity). Enter the child's data in the MyPlate Plan tool and record daily food-group targets.

questions.q: What is energy balance?
questions.a: When calories eaten equal calories used; during adolescence a positive balance is needed to support growth.

questions.q: Roughly how many calories does an active 13–14-year-old need?
questions.a: About 2,000–2,600 for girls and 2,200–3,200 for boys depending on activity (follow the MyPlate Plan result).

days.guide: The child researches calcium, iron and vitamin D and makes a chart of why each matters and three sources.

questions.q: How much calcium do 9–18-year-olds need, and why?
questions.a: 1,300 mg per day; teens build most of their peak bone mass now. Sources: milk, yogurt, cheese, fortified soy milk, tofu made with calcium, kale.

questions.q: Give one source each of iron and vitamin D.
questions.a: Iron: lean red meat, beans, lentils, spinach, fortified cereal. Vitamin D: sunlight, fortified milk, salmon, eggs.

days.guide: The child logs everything eaten for one day and compares food-group amounts with the MyPlate Plan targets.

questions.q: Which food groups did you fall short or go over?
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer compares cup/ounce amounts to the targets for all five groups.

days.guide: Choose the biggest gap and plan three snacks to fill it; check that each snack actually contains the nutrient.

questions.q: Plan a snack to raise calcium.
questions.a: Examples: yogurt with fruit, cheese and whole-grain crackers, a glass of milk or fortified soy milk with a banana.

days.guide: Give the quiz; discuss any misses.

questions.q: What happens if energy intake is consistently too low for an active teen?
questions.a: Fatigue, poor performance, slowed growth, weaker bones, possible missed periods and higher injury risk.

weeks.assessment_key: Food log (4 pts): full day recorded, compared to all 5 groups, gap identified, 3 snacks that address it. Quiz key: 1) energy balance = calories in vs out 2) teens need more energy for growth 3) calcium 1,300 mg/day 4) calcium sources: milk, yogurt, cheese 5) iron carries oxygen in hemoglobin 6) iron sources: meat, beans, spinach, fortified cereal 7) vitamin D helps absorb calcium 8) MyPlate groups: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy 9) half of grains should be whole 10) too little energy: fatigue, slowed growth.

weeks.prep: Collect three magazine ads or social posts with idealized bodies. Read NEDA or KidsHealth eating-disorder fact sheets. Parental preview: discuss eating disorders without numbers (weights, calories) that could be triggering; watch for signs of disordered eating in your own child.
misconceptions: Thinking eating disorders are a choice or only affect thin girls. Correct: they are serious mental illnesses that affect all genders, body sizes and backgrounds.
Believing photos in ads show real bodies. Correct: most are professionally lit, posed and digitally edited.

days.guide: Analyze each ad: Who made it? What is the body message? What might be edited? What is it selling?

questions.q: What clues suggest an image was edited?
questions.a: Unrealistically smooth skin, warped backgrounds near the body, impossible proportions, no pores or stretch marks, inconsistent shadows.

days.guide: Discuss influences (family comments, peers, culture, sports with weight classes or appearance focus). The child writes five positive self-talk statements about what their body can do.

questions.q: Give a positive self-talk statement focused on function, not appearance.
questions.a: Example: 'My legs are strong enough to run a mile,' 'My body lets me play music and hug my family.'

days.guide: Read the fact sheet together and make a chart of anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder: key behaviors and health risks.

questions.q: Describe the three eating disorders.
questions.a: Anorexia: severe restriction and intense fear of weight gain; risks include heart problems, bone loss. Bulimia: binge eating followed by purging (vomiting, laxatives) or excessive exercise; risks include electrolyte imbalance, tooth and throat damage. Binge eating disorder: repeated episodes of eating large amounts with loss of control, without purging; risks include distress, high blood pressure, diabetes.

days.guide: Role-play telling a parent or counselor 'I'm worried about my friend; she's skipping meals and seems upset.' List help sources: trusted adult, doctor, school counselor, NEDA resources.

questions.q: Why tell an adult rather than confront the friend alone?
questions.a: Eating disorders are serious medical and mental illnesses that need professional treatment; a friend cannot fix it, but an adult can get help.

days.guide: The child writes a response to one ad: message, techniques, who benefits and a healthier counter-message.

questions.q: What is a counter-message?
questions.a: A message that challenges the ad's idea, e.g., 'Healthy bodies come in many shapes and sizes.'

weeks.assessment_key: Media-literacy response: 4 = identifies the ad's explicit and implied message, at least two techniques (editing, idealized model, emotional appeal), who profits, and a clear healthy counter-message; 3 = message and one technique plus counter-message; 2 = describes the ad without analysis; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Collect labels (or photos online) of 3 energy drinks and 2 supplements. Print a claim-checking checklist (Who sells it? Evidence? 'Too good to be true'? FDA disclaimer?).
misconceptions: Thinking supplements are FDA-approved for safety and effectiveness before sale. Correct: supplements do not need FDA approval before marketing; the manufacturer is responsible for safety.

Believing energy drinks are a good sports drink. Correct: they contain caffeine and sugar, not appropriate hydration; the American Academy of Pediatrics says children and teens should not have energy drinks.

days.guide: Read labels and record caffeine (mg) and sugar (g) per can. Compare: health experts advise teens limit caffeine to no more than 100 mg/day; the AHA recommends under 25 g added sugar a day for kids.

questions.q: A 16-oz energy drink has 160 mg caffeine and 54 g sugar. How does it compare with teen guidance?
questions.a: Caffeine is about 60 mg over the 100 mg/day guideline, and sugar is more than twice the 25 g limit.

days.guide: Use the checklist on two supplement ads. Look for words like 'miracle,' 'shred fat fast,' before/after photos and paid testimonials.

questions.q: Name two red flags in a supplement ad.
questions.a: Examples: promises of quick or dramatic results, 'secret' or 'miracle' formula, testimonials instead of studies, celebrity endorsements, 'all natural so it's safe.'

days.guide: Explain medicines must be proven safe and effective before FDA approval; supplements do not, and the FDA acts only after problems arise. Read the 'This statement has not been evaluated by the FDA' disclaimer.

questions.q: What does the FDA disclaimer on supplements mean?
questions.a: The FDA has not reviewed the claim; the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent disease.

days.guide: Compare a supplement's claim to the PE fuel plan: carbohydrates for energy, protein from food (meat, eggs, dairy, beans), water, sleep.

questions.q: Do most teen athletes need protein powder?
questions.a: No — most get enough protein from regular meals; food sources provide protein plus other nutrients.

days.guide: The child writes a consumer review of one product claim citing at least two reliable sources (NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, FDA, AAP, KidsHealth).

questions.q: Which is a more reliable source: the product's website or NIH Office of Dietary Supplements? Why?
questions.a: NIH ODS — it is a government health agency with no product to sell and relies on research.

weeks.assessment_key: Consumer review: 4 = states the claim, evaluates it with at least two reliable sources, explains FDA regulation difference, gives a clear verdict and safer alternative; 3 = verdict with one source; 2 = opinion without evidence; 1 = incomplete. Label study: correct caffeine and sugar comparison to 100 mg and 25 g.

weeks.prep: Get a grocery ad or visit a store/website with unit prices. Set a dinner budget (e.g., $20 for four). Choose a recipe and buy ingredients. Write a nutrition unit test (key below).
misconceptions: Thinking healthy food is always expensive. Correct: beans, rice, oats, eggs, frozen vegetables and seasonal produce are cheap and nutritious.
Comparing package price instead of unit price. Correct: divide price by amount to compare value.

days.guide: Teach unit price = price ÷ units. Compare three sizes or brands of a staple (rice, oats, milk).

questions.q: A 2-lb bag of rice costs $3.00 and a 5-lb bag costs $6.50. Which is the better value?
questions.a: 2 lb: $1.50/lb; 5 lb: $1.30/lb. The 5-lb bag is cheaper per pound.

days.guide: The child plans a balanced dinner for four (all or most MyPlate groups) and prices each ingredient to stay under budget.

questions.q: Does your meal include at least four food groups and stay under budget?
questions.a: Answers vary; check the list has protein, grain, vegetable, fruit and/or dairy and that the total is at or under the budget.

days.guide: Cook together. Review clean, separate, cook, chill: wash hands, separate raw meat, use a thermometer (poultry 165°F, ground beef 160°F), refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

questions.q: What is the safe internal temperature for chicken?

days.guide: Read about food insecurity in California and locate the nearest food bank; explain CalFresh (California's SNAP program).

questions.q: What is food insecurity?
questions.a: Lacking consistent access to enough food for an active, healthy life.

questions.q: What is CalFresh?
questions.a: California's name for SNAP, a program that gives eligible households money on an EBT card to buy groceries.

days.guide: Give the unit test; the child also writes a short reflection on the meal (cost, nutrition, what they'd change).

questions.q: Name two ways to save money on healthy food.
questions.a: Compare unit prices, buy in season or frozen, cook at home, plan meals, buy store brands, use beans/eggs as protein.

weeks.assessment_key: Meal plan (4): balanced, priced, under budget, safe-cooking steps noted. Unit test key: 1) energy balance definition 2) calcium 1,300 mg 3) iron and vitamin D roles 4) edited media images are unrealistic 5) anorexia/bulimia/binge eating definitions 6) tell a trusted adult if worried about a friend 7) supplements are not FDA-approved before sale 8) teens: ≤100 mg caffeine, avoid energy drinks 9) unit price calculation 10) chicken 165°F 11) CalFresh = CA SNAP. 80%+ proficient.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: read the unit plan for weeks 11–18 and KidsHealth for Teens sexual health pages. Decide whether to opt out under Ed. Code 51938; if so, use the alternative (puberty, hygiene, healthy friendships). Have a labeled reproductive anatomy diagram from grade 7.
misconceptions: Thinking media portrayals of relationships are realistic. Correct: TV and music often skip consequences, consent and communication.
Believing any website that looks professional is accurate. Correct: check who runs it, evidence, date and purpose (.gov, .edu, medical organizations are more reliable).

days.guide: Sit together and preview topics. Share your family's values and invite questions; record the opt-out decision.

questions.q: Who can you ask when you have questions about growing up and relationships?
questions.a: Parents/guardians, a doctor or nurse, the school counselor, or another trusted adult.

days.guide: Label a male and female reproductive-system diagram and review the role of hormones in puberty.

questions.q: Which hormones drive puberty?
questions.a: Testosterone (mainly in males) and estrogen and progesterone (mainly in females), triggered by signals from the pituitary gland (LH and FSH).

questions.q: Where are eggs produced and where is sperm produced?
questions.a: Eggs mature in the ovaries; sperm are produced in the testes.

days.guide: Pick a TV scene, song or post and compare what it shows with reality (consent, communication, consequences, respect).

questions.q: What do media portrayals of relationships often leave out?
questions.a: Communication, consent, respect, emotional and physical consequences (pregnancy, STIs, heartbreak) and responsibilities.

days.guide: Compare one reliable site (KidsHealth, CDC) with one unreliable site (anonymous forum) on one question using who/what/when/why.

questions.q: Give two signs a health website is reliable.
questions.a: Run by a medical, government or educational organization; cites evidence; recently updated; authors have credentials; not selling products.

days.guide: The child lists three trusted adults and two valid resources, then writes a question for the parent question box.

questions.q: Why is it helpful to have more than one trusted adult?
questions.a: If one is unavailable or the topic feels awkward, another can help.

weeks.assessment_key: Trusted-adult/resource list: 4 = three named trusted adults with roles/contact info, two valid resources (e.g., KidsHealth, CDC, doctor's office) with why they're reliable, and one question submitted; 3 = one missing element; 2 = vague names, unreliable sources; 1 = incomplete. Opted-out students: complete a list of trusted adults and resources for general health questions.

weeks.prep: Parent preview diagrams of fertilization and fetal development (e.g., KidsHealth 'Pregnancy' or a medical textbook). Prepare 8 timeline cards (key below) for the quiz. Opt-out alternative: growth and development across the lifespan timeline.
misconceptions: Believing pregnancy lasts 9 months from conception exactly. Correct: it is about 40 weeks counted from the first day of the last menstrual period (about 38 weeks from fertilization).
Thinking a small amount of alcohol is safe in pregnancy. Correct: no amount of alcohol is known to be safe; it can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.

days.guide: Using the diagram, explain: sperm meets egg in the fallopian tube (fertilization), the zygote divides as it travels, and implants in the uterine lining about 6–10 days later.

questions.q: Where does fertilization usually occur?
questions.a: In the fallopian tube.

questions.q: What is implantation?
questions.a: When the developing ball of cells (blastocyst) attaches to the lining of the uterus.

days.guide: The child builds a three-trimester timeline with key events from a reliable source.

questions.q: Name one milestone in each trimester.
questions.a: 1st (weeks 1–13): heart begins beating around week 5–6, organs begin forming, called a fetus from week 9–10. 2nd (14–27): movement felt, sex can be seen on ultrasound, hearing develops. 3rd (28–40): rapid weight gain, lungs mature, baby turns head-down.

days.guide: Discuss how prenatal care, folic acid, nutrition and avoiding alcohol, tobacco and drugs protect the baby.

questions.q: Why is folic acid important?
questions.a: It helps prevent neural tube defects such as spina bifida; it matters very early, often before a person knows they are pregnant.

questions.q: Name a risk of smoking during pregnancy.
questions.a: Low birth weight, premature birth, miscarriage, SIDS.

days.guide: The child interviews you about responsibilities and costs (time, sleep, money, childcare, emotional demands).

questions.q: Name three responsibilities of raising a child.
questions.a: Examples: providing food, shelter and health care; supervision and time; emotional support; costs of diapers, childcare and education.

days.guide: Give the timeline quiz: the child places cards in order and answers short questions.

questions.q: About how long is a full-term pregnancy?
questions.a: About 40 weeks (counted from the last menstrual period), or roughly 9 months.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline quiz key (correct order): 1) fertilization in fallopian tube 2) implantation in uterus (about 1 week) 3) heartbeat detectable (~6 weeks) 4) embryo becomes fetus (~9–10 weeks) 5) end of 1st trimester (~13 weeks) 6) movement felt (~16–20 weeks) 7) third trimester begins (~28 weeks): lungs mature, weight gain 8) full term ~39–40 weeks. Short answers: no amount of alcohol is safe; prenatal checkups monitor health of parent and baby; folic acid prevents neural tube defects.

weeks.prep: Parent preview the CDC 'Contraception' effectiveness chart (typical-use failure rates). No demonstrations are included. Review a decision-making model (e.g., DECIDE: Define, Explore options, Consider consequences, Identify values, Decide, Evaluate). Opt-out alternative: decision-making on a non-sexual scenario.
misconceptions: Believing any method is 100% effective. Correct: only abstinence is 100% effective at preventing pregnancy and STIs; other methods reduce risk by different amounts.
Thinking hormonal birth control protects against STIs. Correct: only condoms (external/internal) reduce STI risk; hormonal methods and IUDs do not.

days.guide: Discuss what abstinence means and reasons teens choose it (values, health, goals, readiness). Share your family's view.

questions.q: Why is abstinence the only certain way to prevent pregnancy and STIs?
questions.a: If there is no sexual contact, there is no exposure to sperm or to infections passed through sexual contact.

days.guide: Review the chart and discuss typical-use effectiveness (it includes human error). Emphasize the difference between pregnancy and STI protection.

questions.q: Which methods are most effective at preventing pregnancy with typical use?
questions.a: Implant and IUDs (over 99%); sterilization also over 99%.

questions.q: Which method also reduces STI risk?
questions.a: Condoms (external or internal); typical-use pregnancy prevention for external condoms is about 87%.

days.guide: Walk through the decision model on a scenario where a teen is pressured to have sex and wants to wait.

questions.q: Apply one step: what values and consequences should the teen consider?
questions.a: Personal and family values, goals, emotional readiness, risk of pregnancy and STIs, and the right to say no; a healthy partner respects the decision.

days.guide: Have a private conversation about your family's values on relationships and decisions; the child may write a short reflection.

questions.q: What is one value your family holds about relationships?
questions.a: Answers vary; check the child can state it and connect it to decisions.

days.guide: Give short-response questions (key below).

questions.q: Does a hormonal method protect against HIV?
questions.a: No. Only condoms reduce the risk of HIV and other STIs during sex; abstinence eliminates it.

weeks.assessment_key: Short-response key: 1) abstinence is 100% effective at preventing pregnancy and STIs 2) reasons to choose abstinence: values, goals, not ready, avoid risks 3) IUD/implant are most effective reversible methods (>99%) 4) condoms are the only method that also reduce STI risk 5) typical use is lower than perfect use due to human error 6) a partner who pressures you is not respecting you; you can always say no. Proficient = 5 of 6 correct with explanations.

weeks.prep: Parent preview CDC STI fact sheets and HIV.gov 'HIV Basics.' Make 10 fact/myth cards. Look up a local clinic or Planned Parenthood/county clinic. Opt-out alternative: communicable diseases (flu, COVID-19, TB) transmission and prevention.
misconceptions: Believing you can tell if someone has an STI by looking. Correct: many STIs have no symptoms; only testing tells.
Thinking HIV is spread by hugging, sharing drinks or mosquitoes. Correct: HIV is spread through certain body fluids (blood, semen, vaginal fluids, breast milk), mainly through sex or sharing needles.

days.guide: Sort cards: HIV can be spread by sharing needles (fact); by toilet seats (myth); by kissing (myth, essentially no risk); from mother to baby during birth or breastfeeding (fact).

questions.q: Name two ways HIV is transmitted and two ways it is not.
questions.a: Is: sexual contact, sharing needles, from mother to baby (pregnancy, birth, breastfeeding). Is not: hugging, shaking hands, sharing dishes, toilet seats, mosquitoes, saliva/tears/sweat.

days.guide: Explain that chlamydia, gonorrhea, HPV and herpes often cause no symptoms, which is why testing matters.

questions.q: Why can an STI spread even when no one has symptoms?
questions.a: Many infections are asymptomatic, so people don't know they have them and can pass them on; testing is the only way to know.

days.guide: Discuss prevention: abstinence, condoms, mutual monogamy with a tested partner, HPV vaccine, PrEP. Explain bacterial STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) can be cured with antibiotics; viral (HIV, herpes, HPV) can be treated but not cured.

questions.q: Is HIV curable?
questions.a: No, but it is treatable. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) keeps people healthy, and an undetectable viral load means HIV is not transmitted sexually (U=U).

questions.q: What vaccine prevents some STIs?
questions.a: The HPV vaccine prevents infections that cause most cervical and several other cancers and genital warts; the hepatitis B vaccine also helps.

days.guide: Explain California law lets minors 12 and older consent to their own confidential STI testing and treatment. Find a local clinic together.

questions.q: At what age can a California minor consent to STI testing and treatment?
questions.a: 12 and older.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key below).

questions.q: Which STIs can be cured with antibiotics?
questions.a: Bacterial ones: chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis (also trichomoniasis, a parasite, with medicine).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) many STIs have no symptoms – true 2) HIV spread by sharing needles – true 3) HIV spread by hugging – false 4) abstinence is the only 100% prevention 5) condoms reduce risk of HIV and many STIs 6) bacterial STIs cured by antibiotics: chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis 7) HIV, herpes, HPV are viral, treatable not curable 8) HPV vaccine prevents cancer-causing HPV 9) testing is the only way to know status 10) CA minors 12+ can consent to confidential STI services. 8/10 proficient.

weeks.prep: Read the CHYA-aligned glossary (e.g., from your county or the CA Department of Education/KidsHealth 'Sexual Orientation' and 'Gender Identity'). Prepare scenario cards about identity-based teasing. Discuss family values beforehand; the lesson's focus is respect and safety for all.
misconceptions: Confusing gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation. Correct: identity is one's internal sense of gender; expression is how it is shown outwardly; orientation is who one is attracted to.
Thinking jokes about identity are harmless. Correct: identity-based bullying is linked to depression, anxiety and higher suicide risk; it also violates school policy and California law.

days.guide: Read each term from the glossary and the child explains it in their own words; talk about questions with you.

questions.q: Define gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation.
questions.a: Gender identity: a person's internal sense of their own gender. Gender expression: how a person shows gender outwardly (clothing, hair, behavior). Sexual orientation: who a person is emotionally, romantically or physically attracted to.

days.guide: Look at toy aisles, ads or shows and list stereotypes (e.g., 'boys don't cry,' 'girls aren't good at science'). Discuss how they limit choices.

questions.q: How can gender stereotypes limit people?
questions.a: They pressure people into narrow roles and discourage interests, careers or emotions that don't fit the stereotype.

days.guide: Discuss the harm of identity-based bullying and model upstander responses: 'That's not cool,' check on the target, report to an adult.

questions.q: Name two upstander responses.
questions.a: Speak up calmly, support the person being targeted afterward, don't laugh or share, report to a trusted adult or school.

days.guide: List supportive resources: trusted adults, school counselor, doctor, The Trevor Project (crisis support for LGBTQ+ youth), 988.

questions.q: Where can a teen with questions about identity find support?
questions.a: A parent or trusted adult, school counselor, doctor, or confidential lines such as The Trevor Project or 988.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph explaining how to treat all people with dignity and respect, with two concrete actions.

questions.q: What does treating someone with dignity look like at school?
questions.a: Using kind words and people's names, including others, not spreading rumors or jokes, and standing up when someone is mistreated.

weeks.assessment_key: Respect paragraph: 4 = clear claim that all people deserve dignity, accurate use of at least two terms, two concrete actions (upstander response, inclusive language), mention of harm caused by bullying; 3 = clear with one action; 2 = general statement only; 1 = incomplete or disrespectful.

weeks.prep: Print the loveisrespect.org relationship spectrum (healthy, unhealthy, abusive). Prepare 12 behavior cards. Choose a short story or scenario with a teen relationship (or write one) for Friday.
misconceptions: Thinking jealousy and constant texting show love. Correct: monitoring, jealousy and control are red flags, not signs of caring.
Believing silence or not saying no equals consent. Correct: consent is a clear, freely given yes, can be withdrawn at any time, and cannot be given if someone is pressured, asleep, or intoxicated.

days.guide: Sort behavior cards onto the spectrum (e.g., respects boundaries = healthy; guilt-trips = unhealthy; hits, threatens or controls money = abusive).

questions.q: Place 'checks your phone without asking' on the spectrum.
questions.a: Unhealthy to abusive — it is controlling and violates privacy, especially if it is repeated or demanded.

days.guide: List digital red flags and discuss what to do (talk to a trusted adult, set boundaries, block, save evidence).

questions.q: Name three digital red flags.
questions.a: Demanding passwords, checking location, constant texting and anger if you don't reply, pressuring for photos, posting private information, controlling who you follow.

days.guide: Teach consent as clear, freely given, ongoing and reversible using everyday examples (borrowing a phone, a hug) and age-appropriate relationship scenarios.

questions.q: If someone said yes earlier but now says stop, what must happen?
questions.a: Stop immediately — consent can be withdrawn at any time.

questions.q: Can a person who is pressured or drunk give consent?
questions.a: No. Consent must be freely given by someone able to make the choice.

days.guide: Practice refusal phrases ('No, I'm not comfortable with that') and negotiation ('I don't want to __, but we could __'). Use firm voice and body language.

questions.q: Give a refusal line and a negotiation line.
questions.a: Refusal: 'No. I'm not ready, and I need you to respect that.' Negotiation: 'I don't want to go to that party, but we could see a movie with friends.'

days.guide: Read the story; the child lists healthy and unhealthy behaviors with evidence and suggests what the character could do.

questions.q: What makes a relationship healthy?
questions.a: Respect, trust, honesty, good communication, equality, and each person keeps their own friends and interests.

weeks.assessment_key: Relationship analysis: 4 = at least three healthy and three unhealthy/abusive behaviors with evidence from the story, correctly placed on the spectrum, and a realistic action step (talk to trusted adult, loveisrespect.org); 3 = two of each plus action; 2 = lists without evidence; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: read CA DOJ human-trafficking pages and NCMEC 'Take It Down' (takeitdown.ncmec.org). Note the National Human Trafficking Hotline 1-888-373-7888 (text 233733). Reassure the child they will never be in trouble for telling you.
misconceptions: Thinking trafficking always involves strangers kidnapping someone. Correct: most victims are recruited by someone they know or meet online, using manipulation, not force.
Believing a sextortion victim should pay or stay silent. Correct: it is never the victim's fault; stop responding, don't pay, save evidence, tell an adult and report.

days.guide: Define trafficking as using force, fraud or coercion to exploit someone for labor or commercial sex (any commercial sex involving a minor is trafficking). Note it happens in California, often by someone known.

questions.q: What is human trafficking?
questions.a: Exploiting a person for labor or commercial sex through force, fraud or coercion; any minor involved in commercial sex is a victim of trafficking regardless of force.

days.guide: List grooming steps: targeting, gaining trust, filling a need (gifts, attention), isolating, secrecy, control.

questions.q: Name three grooming red flags.
questions.a: Excessive gifts or attention, asking to keep things secret, trying to isolate you from family/friends, moving the chat to private apps, asking for photos, promising jobs or modeling deals.

days.guide: Explain sextortion (threats to share images unless you send money or more images). Teach: stop responding, don't pay, save evidence (screenshots, usernames), tell an adult, report to NCMEC (CyberTipline) and use Take It Down.

questions.q: What are the steps if someone threatens to share an image of you?
questions.a: Stop responding, don't pay or send more, save evidence, block after saving, tell a trusted adult, report to the platform and NCMEC CyberTipline, and use Take It Down to help remove images.

days.guide: Role-play telling you about an uncomfortable online contact. Write the National Human Trafficking Hotline number.

questions.q: What is the National Human Trafficking Hotline?
questions.a: 1-888-373-7888, or text 233733; call 911 in immediate danger.

days.guide: The child makes a tip card for younger teens with red flags, steps and contacts.

questions.q: Whose fault is sextortion?
questions.a: Never the victim's — the person making threats is committing a crime.

weeks.assessment_key: Safety tip card: 4 = accurate definition, at least three grooming red flags, sextortion steps (stop, don't pay, save evidence, tell, report/Take It Down), hotline number and trusted adult, age-appropriate wording; 3 = one element missing; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Prepare three relationship scenario cards, vocabulary flashcards from weeks 11–17 and the unit test (key below). Opted-out students: alternative test on puberty, hygiene and healthy friendships.
misconceptions: Thinking decisions now don't affect the future. Correct: choices about relationships and risk can affect health, education and goals.
Forgetting that refusing pressure is a skill that takes practice. Correct: rehearse words and plans in advance.

days.guide: The child applies the decision model to three scenarios, writing options, consequences and the healthy choice.

questions.q: A partner says 'If you loved me you would.' What is happening and what is a healthy response?
questions.a: Pressure/manipulation. Healthy response: a clear refusal ('No. Loving me means respecting my answer') and talking to a trusted adult if pressure continues.

days.guide: The child writes how relationship decisions now could affect school, sports and career goals.

questions.q: Give one way an early pregnancy or STI could affect future goals.
questions.a: It could interrupt school or sports, add financial and caregiving responsibilities, or create long-term health effects.

days.guide: The child writes and rehearses a script to raise a relationship question with you.

questions.q: What's a good opening line?
questions.a: Example: 'Can I ask you something kind of awkward? I want your advice about a friend situation.'

days.guide: Quiz vocabulary with flashcards: consent, abstinence, STI, HIV, implantation, trimester, grooming, sextortion, gender identity.

questions.q: Define affirmative consent.
questions.a: A clear, voluntary, ongoing agreement to engage in an activity, which can be withdrawn at any time.

days.guide: Give the unit test closed-book and review answers.

questions.q: What is the only 100% effective way to avoid pregnancy and STIs?
questions.a: Abstinence.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: 1) fertilization in fallopian tube 2) pregnancy ~40 weeks, three trimesters 3) no safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy 4) abstinence 100% effective 5) condoms reduce STI risk; hormonal methods don't 6) many STIs have no symptoms 7) HIV treatable with ART, not curable 8) CA minors 12+ can consent to STI testing 9) definitions of gender identity, expression, orientation 10) consent is clear, ongoing, can be withdrawn 11) digital red flags: password demands, tracking 12) sextortion steps: stop, don't pay, save evidence, tell, report 13) trafficking hotline 1-888-373-7888. Alternative test: puberty changes, daily hygiene, qualities of healthy friendships.

weeks.prep: Print a BAC factor chart and the CA DMV handbook section on alcohol and driving. Set up a straight tape line on the floor for the impairment activity. Write a 5-question recap quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking coffee, a cold shower or food 'sobers you up.' Correct: only time lowers BAC; the liver removes alcohol at a fixed rate (about one standard drink per hour).
Believing a person 'seems fine' so they can drive. Correct: judgment and reaction time are impaired before obvious signs appear.

days.guide: Give a quick 5-question recap (alcohol is a depressant; affects brain, liver, heart; slows reaction time; teen brain still developing).

questions.q: Is alcohol a stimulant or depressant?
questions.a: A depressant — it slows the central nervous system.

days.guide: Explain BAC is the percent of alcohol in the blood. Go over factors: body size, sex (body water and enzymes), food in stomach, number of drinks and time. Explain the developing prefrontal cortex and hippocampus are more vulnerable.

questions.q: Why would the same number of drinks give a smaller person a higher BAC?
questions.a: Less body mass and water to dilute the alcohol, so the concentration in the blood is higher.

questions.q: Which part of the brain, still developing in teens, controls judgment?
questions.a: The prefrontal cortex (develops into the mid-20s).

days.guide: Have the child walk the tape line while counting backward by 7s from 100, then try with a spinning or eye-cover challenge (with a spotter). Discuss how divided attention and impaired balance compare to drinking.

questions.q: What did the activity show about impairment?
questions.a: Balance, coordination and attention worsen together, and you can't fully judge your own impairment.

days.guide: Read the DMV section: drivers under 21 may not drive with BAC 0.01% or higher (zero tolerance); the adult limit is 0.08%. Discuss social host liability for adults who give alcohol to minors.

questions.q: What is California's BAC limit for drivers under 21?
questions.a: 0.01% (zero tolerance); drivers 21+ are illegal at 0.08% or higher. Refusing a chemical test or a BAC of 0.01%+ leads to license suspension.

days.guide: The child writes a safe-ride plan: don't get in, call a parent (no-questions-asked agreement), code word, ride-share with parent's account, stay over.

questions.q: Your ride has been drinking. What do you do?
questions.a: Do not get in; call or text a parent or trusted adult for a ride, use a code word if needed, and stay with sober friends until help arrives.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) depressant 2) only time lowers BAC 3) factors: weight, sex, food, number of drinks, time 4) prefrontal cortex develops into mid-20s 5) CA under-21 limit 0.01%, adults 0.08%. Safe-ride plan (4): refuses ride, names two alternatives, contact numbers, code word/agreement with parent.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: overdose content. Watch a naloxone (Narcan) nasal-spray training video (SAMHSA, CDPH or manufacturer) first. Use a doll or pillow and an empty spray bottle as a model. Learn California's Good Samaritan law (Health & Safety Code 11376.5).
misconceptions: Thinking pills from friends or social media are safe if they look real. Correct: counterfeit pills often contain fentanyl; one pill can kill.
Believing naloxone is dangerous if the person didn't take opioids. Correct: naloxone has no effect on someone without opioids in their system and is safe to give if overdose is suspected.

days.guide: Explain opioids (oxycodone, heroin, fentanyl) bind receptors in the brainstem and slow breathing; fentanyl is 50 times stronger than heroin and 2 mg can be fatal.

questions.q: Why do opioid overdoses kill?
questions.a: Opioids slow or stop breathing, so the brain and body don't get oxygen.

questions.q: Why are counterfeit pills so dangerous?
questions.a: They can contain unknown, lethal amounts of fentanyl and look identical to real prescription pills.

days.guide: List overdose signs together: pinpoint pupils, unresponsive/can't wake, slow or stopped breathing, gurgling/snoring sounds, blue or gray lips/fingertips, limp body.

questions.q: Name three signs of opioid overdose.
questions.a: Pinpoint pupils, unresponsiveness, slow or no breathing, blue/gray lips or nails, choking or gurgling sounds, limp body.

days.guide: Watch the video, then practice: shout and rub sternum, call 911, tilt head back, insert nozzle into a nostril and press plunger, place in recovery position, give second dose in 2–3 minutes if no response, stay until help arrives.

questions.q: After giving naloxone, what next?
questions.a: Stay with the person, give rescue breathing/CPR if trained and needed, put them in the recovery position, and give a second dose after 2–3 minutes if they don't respond; naloxone can wear off, so they still need medical care.

days.guide: Explain the Good Samaritan law: a person who seeks medical help for an overdose is protected from arrest/prosecution for small amounts of drugs for personal use.

questions.q: Why does California have a Good Samaritan overdose law?
questions.a: To encourage people to call 911 without fear of being arrested for minor drug possession, saving lives.

days.guide: The child orders shuffled step cards for responding to an overdose and explains each.

questions.q: What is the first thing to do if someone won't wake up?
questions.a: Try to wake them (shout, rub sternum) and call 911 immediately.

weeks.assessment_key: Correct sequence: 1) Check responsiveness (shout, sternum rub) 2) Call 911 3) Give naloxone into one nostril 4) Support breathing (rescue breaths/CPR if trained) 5) Recovery position on side 6) Second dose after 2–3 minutes if no response 7) Stay until EMS arrives and tell them what happened. Proficient: all steps in order with reasons.

weeks.prep: Print NIDA for Teens pages on prescription stimulants, inhalants, caffeine and marijuana. Make a blank drug-facts chart (drug, effects, risks, CA law). Have energy-drink/soda labels for caffeine counts.
misconceptions: Thinking prescription drugs are safe because a doctor prescribed them. Correct: safe only for the person prescribed at the right dose; misuse can cause heart problems, addiction and overdose.
Believing cannabis today is the same as decades ago. Correct: THC potency has risen from about 4% in the 1990s to often 20%+ in flower and 60–90%+ in concentrates/vapes.

days.guide: Explain ADHD stimulants (Adderall, Ritalin) help people with ADHD but misuse can cause rapid heart rate, anxiety, insomnia and addiction; sharing or selling a prescription is illegal.

questions.q: Do 'study drugs' improve grades for people without ADHD?
questions.a: Research shows no real improvement in grades; they carry risks such as heart problems, anxiety and dependence.

days.guide: Read about inhalants (aerosols, glue, gasoline). Explain 'sudden sniffing death' can happen the first time from heart failure.

questions.q: How can inhalants kill on first use?
questions.a: They can cause the heart to beat irregularly and stop (sudden sniffing death), or cause suffocation.

days.guide: The child lists all caffeine for a typical week (soda ~35–45 mg/12 oz, tea ~30–50 mg/8 oz, coffee ~95 mg/8 oz, energy drinks 80–300 mg) and compares to ≤100 mg/day.

questions.q: A teen drinks two 12-oz colas (35 mg each) and one 8-oz coffee (95 mg) in a day. Is that over 100 mg?
questions.a: Yes: 35 + 35 + 95 = 165 mg, which is 65 mg over 100 mg.

days.guide: Compare THC levels then and now and discuss risks to the teen brain: memory, attention, mood, addiction (cannabis use disorder), psychosis risk with high-potency use; illegal under 21 in CA.

questions.q: Why are high-potency vapes and edibles riskier for teens?
questions.a: Higher THC raises risk of addiction, anxiety, psychosis and impaired memory/learning; edibles take 30 minutes–2 hours to work, leading people to take too much.

days.guide: The child fills the drug-facts chart for stimulants, inhalants, caffeine and cannabis.

questions.q: What is California's legal age for cannabis?
questions.a: 21 (18 with a medical recommendation).

weeks.assessment_key: Drug-facts chart key: Prescription stimulants – increase alertness/heart rate; risks: heart problems, anxiety, insomnia, addiction; sharing/selling is illegal. Inhalants – brief high; risks: brain damage, sudden sniffing death, suffocation; selling certain products to minors is restricted. Caffeine – stimulant; risks: jitters, insomnia, rapid heartbeat; teens ≤100 mg/day, avoid energy drinks. Cannabis – THC alters perception/memory; risks: addiction, impaired learning, psychosis; illegal under 21. Proficient: accurate in all four rows.

weeks.prep: Find 2–3 online examples of vape, alcohol or cannabis ads (or Truth Initiative examples). Print a media-literacy checklist (who made it, target audience, techniques, what's left out). Read about California's flavored tobacco ban (SB 793, upheld by voters with Prop 31 in 2022).
misconceptions: Thinking ads only target adults. Correct: flavors, bright packaging, cartoons and influencers appeal to youth, who are 'replacement customers.'
Believing vapes are just water vapor. Correct: aerosol contains nicotine, heavy metals and ultrafine particles.

days.guide: List tactics: flavors (candy, fruit), influencer posts, sleek packaging, sponsorships of events/music, small discreet devices, 'free' samples.

questions.q: Why do companies use sweet flavors?
questions.a: Flavors hide the harsh taste and appeal especially to young people, making it easier to start.

days.guide: Analyze two ads with the checklist and write findings.

questions.q: What does an alcohol ad usually leave out?
questions.a: Risks: hangovers, impaired driving, addiction, health problems, violence, and the legal age.

days.guide: Explain the flavored tobacco ban: California prohibits retail sale of most flavored tobacco products, including menthol and flavored vapes, approved by voters (Prop 31) in 2022.

questions.q: Why did California ban flavored tobacco sales?
questions.a: Most youth who use tobacco start with flavored products; the ban aims to reduce youth vaping and smoking.

days.guide: The child sketches a counter-ad that exposes one tactic (e.g., 'They flavor it like candy because they want kids hooked').

questions.q: What makes a counter-ad effective?
questions.a: It reveals the hidden tactic or truth, targets the audience clearly and uses a strong image and short message.

days.guide: The child presents the counter-ad and explains the tactic and evidence.

questions.q: Who are 'replacement smokers'?
questions.a: Young people the industry needs to recruit to replace customers who quit or die.

weeks.assessment_key: Counter-ad rubric: 4 = names a specific tactic, accurate fact, clear target audience, strong visual and slogan, explained confidently; 3 = tactic and message clear, weaker design; 2 = general anti-drug message without tactic; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Read NIDA for Teens 'Drugs and the Brain' and a recovery story (NIDA, SAMHSA or a reputable news profile). Health journal ready.
misconceptions: Thinking addiction is a lack of willpower. Correct: it is a chronic, treatable brain disease involving changes in reward, motivation and self-control circuits.
Believing relapse means treatment failed. Correct: relapse rates are similar to other chronic diseases like asthma; it signals a need to adjust treatment.

days.guide: Explain dopamine and the reward system, tolerance (needing more for the same effect) and dependence/withdrawal.

questions.q: What is tolerance?
questions.a: When the body adapts so a person needs more of a drug to get the same effect.

days.guide: Explain why addiction is called a chronic disease: lasting brain changes, compulsive use despite harm, can be managed but relapse is possible.

questions.q: Why is addiction called a disease rather than a choice?
questions.a: Repeated use changes brain circuits for reward, stress and self-control, making it very hard to stop even when the person wants to; the first use is a choice, but addiction is not.

days.guide: The child researches treatments: counseling/behavioral therapy, medications (e.g., buprenorphine, methadone, naltrexone for opioids), support groups, inpatient/outpatient.

questions.q: Name two types of addiction treatment.
questions.a: Behavioral counseling (e.g., CBT), medication for opioid use disorder, support groups (12-step, SMART Recovery), residential or outpatient programs.

days.guide: Read or watch a recovery story and list supports that helped (family, treatment, new friends, purpose).

questions.q: What supports help people stay in recovery?
questions.a: Ongoing treatment, supportive family and friends, sober activities, support groups, coping skills and purpose.

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph explaining addiction to a younger student in simple words.

questions.q: What's a simple way to explain addiction?
questions.a: 'Drugs can change how your brain works so it feels like you need them, even when they hurt you. It's a sickness that doctors can help treat.'

weeks.assessment_key: Explanatory paragraph: 4 = explains dopamine/reward and tolerance in simple terms, calls addiction a treatable disease, mentions treatment and where to get help, age-appropriate; 3 = accurate with one gap; 2 = mostly 'just say no' without explanation; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Prepare scenario cards and a jeopardy grid (categories: Alcohol, Opioids, Other Drugs, Marketing, Addiction). Note SAMHSA National Helpline 1-800-662-4357. Write the unit test.
misconceptions: Thinking telling an adult is 'snitching.' Correct: getting help for a friend's health and safety is caring, not betrayal.
Confronting a friend while they are high. Correct: talk when they are sober, in private, using I-messages.

days.guide: List signs a friend may be using: changes in friends, grades, mood, sleep, secrecy, smell, missing money, paraphernalia.

questions.q: Name three signs.
questions.a: Dropping grades, new friend group, mood swings, secrecy, red eyes or smell of smoke/vape, losing interest in activities, missing money.

days.guide: Teach I-messages ('I feel worried when I see you vaping before school because I care about you'). Role-play; switch roles.

questions.q: Write an I-message for a friend who's drinking at parties.
questions.a: 'I feel worried when you drink at parties because I care about you and don't want you to get hurt. Can we talk?'

days.guide: List adults (parent, counselor, coach, doctor) and hotlines: SAMHSA 1-800-662-4357, 911 in emergencies.

questions.q: What is the SAMHSA National Helpline?
questions.a: 1-800-662-HELP (4357), free, confidential, 24/7 treatment referral and information.

days.guide: Play jeopardy reviewing weeks 19–23.

questions.q: What drug can reverse an opioid overdose?
questions.a: Naloxone (Narcan).

days.guide: Give the unit test; review.

questions.q: What does the Good Samaritan law do?
questions.a: Protects people who call 911 for an overdose from arrest for small-amount drug possession.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: 1) only time lowers BAC 2) under-21 driving limit 0.01% 3) fentanyl in counterfeit pills 4) overdose signs: pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, unresponsive 5) naloxone steps 6) Good Samaritan law 7) inhalants can cause sudden death 8) teen caffeine ≤100 mg 9) higher THC potency risks 10) marketing tactics: flavors, influencers 11) CA flavored tobacco ban 12) addiction = chronic treatable brain disease 13) tolerance definition 14) I-messages and telling an adult. Role-play: proficient = I-message, caring tone, offers help, involves adult.

weeks.prep: Watch the AHA Hands-Only CPR video (cpr.heart.org) together. Use a firm pillow or manikin on the floor. Pick a song at 100–120 bpm ('Stayin' Alive'). Find an AED demonstration video. Print a CPR skills checklist.
misconceptions: Compressing too gently or too slowly. Correct: push hard (at least 2 inches for adults) and fast (100–120/min), letting the chest recoil fully.
Fearing you'll hurt someone or get sued. Correct: without CPR the person will likely die; California's Good Samaritan laws protect people giving emergency care in good faith.

days.guide: Review Check (scene safe, tap and shout), Call (911, get AED), Care. Practice a 911 script: location, what happened, breathing status.

questions.q: What should you tell the 911 dispatcher?
questions.a: Exact location, what happened, number of victims, whether the person is conscious and breathing; stay on the line and follow instructions.

days.guide: Practice hand position (heel of hand on center of chest, other hand on top, arms straight) and compressions to the beat for 2 minutes.

questions.q: What are the two steps of hands-only CPR?
questions.a: Call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100–120 compressions per minute, at least 2 inches deep for adults.

questions.q: When can you stop?
questions.a: When EMS or someone trained takes over, an AED is ready, the person starts breathing, the scene becomes unsafe or you're too exhausted to continue.

days.guide: Watch the AED video. The child sequences: turn on, follow voice prompts, bare chest, attach pads, stand clear for analysis, press shock if advised, resume CPR immediately.

questions.q: What is the first step when an AED arrives?
questions.a: Turn it on and follow the voice prompts.

days.guide: Teach the universal choking sign (hands at throat). Ask 'Are you choking?' Show hand placement for abdominal thrusts (fist above navel, below ribs) without real thrusts.

questions.q: If someone can cough forcefully, what should you do?
questions.a: Encourage them to keep coughing; give abdominal thrusts only if they can't cough, speak or breathe.

days.guide: Run a scenario: someone collapses. The parent checks each step on the checklist.

questions.q: Why start compressions right away?
questions.a: Brain damage begins within minutes without oxygen; compressions circulate oxygenated blood until help arrives.

weeks.assessment_key: CPR skills checklist (1 pt each): checks scene safety; taps and shouts; calls 911 and sends for AED; correct hand position; rate 100–120/min; depth ~2 inches with full recoil; minimal interruptions; uses AED steps correctly; states choking sign and thrust placement. 8–9 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Bookmark AirNow.gov and a first-aid guide (Red Cross app). Learn rip-current escape. Write a scenario quiz (key below).
misconceptions: Thinking heat stroke victims always sweat. Correct: in heat stroke, skin may be hot and dry or still sweaty; confusion and body temperature of 103°F+ are key — call 911.
Swimming straight back to shore against a rip current. Correct: swim parallel to shore until out of the current, or float and signal for help.

days.guide: Compare heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, nausea, dizziness) and heat stroke (high body temp, confusion, hot skin, possible fainting). First aid: move to cool place, loosen clothing, cool with water; heat stroke = call 911 and cool rapidly.

questions.q: What's the main difference and what do you do for heat stroke?
questions.a: Heat stroke involves very high body temperature and confusion/altered mental status; it is a medical emergency — call 911 and cool the person rapidly (cold water, ice packs).

days.guide: Teach reach-throw-don't go: reach with a pole or towel, throw a flotation device, don't swim out. Show how a rip current looks and how to escape.

questions.q: How do you escape a rip current?
questions.a: Stay calm, don't fight it; swim parallel to the shore until out of the current, then swim back at an angle, or float/tread water and wave for help.

days.guide: Check today's AQI on AirNow and learn the color scale (0–50 good, 51–100 moderate, 101–150 unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151+ unhealthy).

questions.q: At what AQI should sensitive groups limit outdoor activity?
questions.a: Above 100 (orange, unhealthy for sensitive groups); above 150 everyone should reduce outdoor exertion.

days.guide: The child writes a family plan: cooling spots, water, check on elderly neighbors, close windows, HEPA/air purifier, N95 masks, indoor activities.

questions.q: Name two steps for a wildfire smoke day.
questions.a: Stay indoors with windows closed, run a HEPA air purifier or AC on recirculate, wear a well-fitted N95 outdoors, avoid exercise outside.

days.guide: Give the scenario quiz.

questions.q: A teammate is confused and has hot skin after practice in the heat. What do you do?
questions.a: Suspect heat stroke: call 911, move them to shade, cool them rapidly with water/ice, and stay with them.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key: 1) heavy sweating, nausea, dizziness = heat exhaustion: move to cool place, fluids, rest 2) confusion and very high temp = heat stroke: 911 + rapid cooling 3) friend struggling in a pool: reach or throw, don't go 4) caught in rip current: swim parallel to shore 5) AQI 160: everyone limit outdoor activity 6) smoke day: stay inside, HEPA, N95 outdoors. 5/6 proficient.

weeks.prep: Find teen pedestrian/cyclist data (NHTSA or CA Office of Traffic Safety). Set up a cone (or shoe) path for the distraction test. Check bike and helmet fit.
misconceptions: Thinking pedestrians and cyclists are always seen by drivers. Correct: drivers have blind spots and may be distracted; make eye contact and wear bright/reflective gear.
Believing you can text and walk safely. Correct: distraction reduces awareness and slows reaction time.

days.guide: Read the data together and identify patterns (time of day, distraction, ages, helmet use).

questions.q: When are pedestrian deaths most common?
questions.a: After dark (most occur at night) and in urban areas away from intersections.

days.guide: The child walks the cone path once normally and once while typing a message; record errors and time.

questions.q: What did the distraction test show?
questions.a: More errors (hitting cones, drifting) and/or slower time while texting — attention can't fully focus on two tasks.

days.guide: Sit in the driver's seat of a parked car with the child walking around it to find blind spots (behind, sides, in front of large vehicles).

questions.q: How can a cyclist be more visible?
questions.a: Wear bright/reflective clothing, use front white light and rear red reflector/light at night, ride predictably with traffic, make eye contact with drivers.

days.guide: Agree on a family code word and no-questions-asked pickup. Practice refusing a ride from a distracted or impaired driver.

questions.q: What might you say to refuse a ride?
questions.a: 'No thanks, my mom is picking me up,' or text the code word to a parent.

days.guide: The child creates a walking/biking safety checklist.

questions.q: Does California require helmets for cyclists under 18?
questions.a: Yes — riders under 18 must wear a helmet on a bicycle, scooter, skateboard or skates.

weeks.assessment_key: Safety checklist: 4 = at least 8 accurate items covering helmet (required under 18 in CA), visibility, phone away, crosswalks and eye contact, riding with traffic, lights at night, safe-ride code word; 3 = 6–7 items; 2 = 4–5; 1 = fewer.

weeks.prep: Prepare scenario cards (in person and online harassment). Read loveisrespect.org and the 5 D's (Right To Be/Hollaback). Know how your school or co-op reports harassment.
misconceptions: Thinking harassment only counts if it's physical. Correct: unwelcome comments, jokes, gestures, images or messages of a sexual nature are harassment.
Believing bystanders can only confront directly. Correct: the 5 D's give safer options.

days.guide: Define sexual harassment and list examples in person and online.

questions.q: Give two examples of online sexual harassment.
questions.a: Sending unwanted sexual messages or images, spreading sexual rumors, sharing someone's photo without consent, sexual comments on posts.

days.guide: Teach the 5 D's: Direct, Distract, Delegate, Delay, Document.

questions.q: Explain 'Delegate' and 'Delay.'
questions.a: Delegate: get help from someone with authority (teacher, coach, adult). Delay: check in with the person afterward to support them.

days.guide: Role-play three scenarios using different D's.

questions.q: Someone is being teased in a group chat. What could you do?
questions.a: Distract by changing the subject, message the target privately (Delay), screenshot (Document), and tell an adult (Delegate).

days.guide: List reporting options: parent, school counselor/Title IX coordinator, platform reports, police for assault, RAINN hotline 1-800-656-4673.

questions.q: Where can someone report sexual assault?
questions.a: Tell a trusted adult, call 911 or police, contact RAINN 1-800-656-HOPE (4673), or a school Title IX coordinator.

days.guide: The child writes how they would support a friend who was harassed.

questions.q: What should you say first to a friend who discloses harassment or assault?
questions.a: 'I believe you. It's not your fault. I'm here for you,' then help them get adult support.

weeks.assessment_key: Bystander role-play rubric: 4 = uses at least two D's appropriately, prioritizes safety, supports the target and involves an adult; 3 = one D used well; 2 = hesitant/unsafe; 1 = no action. Reflection: believes, supports, connects to help.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: weapons and threats. Review Sandy Hook Promise 'Say Something' resources. Know whether firearms are in your home or relatives' homes and how they're stored. Prepare scenario cards.
misconceptions: Thinking a found gun is safe to pick up if it looks like a toy or unloaded. Correct: never touch it — leave the area and tell an adult.
Believing threats online are 'just jokes.' Correct: always report threats; adults will assess them.

days.guide: Teach: Stop, don't touch, leave the area, tell an adult. Explain safe storage (locked, unloaded, ammunition separate).

questions.q: You find a gun at a friend's house. What do you do?
questions.a: Don't touch it, leave the room/area immediately, and tell an adult right away.

days.guide: List warning signs someone may hurt themselves or others: threats, fascination with weapons/violence, withdrawal, posts about violence, severe anger.

questions.q: Name two warning signs of potential violence.
questions.a: Making threats (in person or online), talking about bringing a weapon, obsession with weapons or past attacks, sudden withdrawal and anger, social posts about hurting others.

days.guide: Practice showing a parent a screenshot of a threat and explaining it. Learn anonymous options (Say Something app, school tip line, 911 if imminent).

questions.q: If you see a threat online, what should you do?
questions.a: Don't share it; screenshot it, tell a trusted adult immediately or use an anonymous tip line; call 911 if there's immediate danger.

days.guide: Practice de-escalation: calm low voice, give space, don't block exits, acknowledge feelings, walk away and get help.

questions.q: Name two de-escalation strategies.
questions.a: Speak calmly, keep a safe distance, listen and acknowledge feelings, avoid insults or threats, leave and get an adult.

days.guide: The child completes a scenario worksheet.

questions.q: Why report even if you aren't sure it's serious?
questions.a: Adults trained to assess threats can decide; reporting may prevent harm and get help for the person.
