weeks.assessment_key: Scenario worksheet key: 1) found gun – don't touch, leave, tell adult 2) classmate posts a threat – screenshot, tell adult/tip line 3) friend talks about hurting themselves – Ask-Listen-Tell, 988 4) heated argument – calm voice, space, leave 5) imminent danger – 911. Proficient: all five correct.

weeks.prep: Gather a first-aid kit and the Red Cross checklist, a CPR pillow, flashcards and the unit test (key below).
misconceptions: Thinking a family plan isn't needed because 911 exists. Correct: phones and roads can fail; you need meeting places and out-of-area contacts.
Forgetting that supplies expire. Correct: check dates and restock regularly.

days.guide: Inventory the kit against a Red Cross list (bandages, gauze, tape, gloves, antiseptic wipes, scissors, tweezers, thermometer, cold pack, emergency blanket) and list items to buy.

questions.q: Why include disposable gloves?
questions.a: To protect against contact with blood and body fluids.

days.guide: Create a plan: emergency contacts, out-of-area contact, meeting place near home and outside neighborhood, evacuation routes, go-bag.

questions.q: Why choose an out-of-area contact?
questions.a: Long-distance calls/texts may get through when local lines are overloaded; everyone can check in with one person.

days.guide: The child demonstrates hands-only CPR and choking response; check with the week 25 checklist.

questions.q: What is the compression rate?
questions.a: 100–120 per minute.

days.guide: Review flashcards for weeks 25–29.

questions.q: Reach, throw, don't ___?
questions.a: Go — don't swim out to rescue someone unless trained.

days.guide: Give the unit test.

questions.q: What do the 5 D's stand for?
questions.a: Direct, Distract, Delegate, Delay, Document.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit test key: 1) Check-Call-Care 2) CPR 100–120/min, ~2 in 3) AED: turn on first 4) choking sign = hands at throat 5) heat stroke = 911 6) rip current: swim parallel 7) AQI >150 unhealthy for all 8) helmet required under 18 9) 5 D's 10) found gun: don't touch, leave, tell 11) threats: report. Skills demo: proficient on week 25 checklist.

weeks.prep: Print a family health history form (CDC 'My Family Health Portrait') and CDC fact sheets on heart disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer and asthma. Be ready to share family history sensitively.
misconceptions: Thinking chronic diseases only affect old people. Correct: habits started in youth (diet, activity, tobacco) shape lifetime risk; type 2 diabetes and asthma occur in teens.
Believing family history means you're destined to get a disease. Correct: it raises risk, but controllable behaviors can lower it.

days.guide: Review communicable vs. noncommunicable diseases and list chronic examples.

questions.q: Name four chronic noncommunicable diseases.
questions.a: Heart disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer, asthma (also stroke, COPD, arthritis).

days.guide: Sort risk factors: controllable (diet, activity, tobacco, sleep, sun exposure) vs. uncontrollable (age, genetics, family history, sex).

questions.q: Is family history controllable?
questions.a: No — but knowing it helps you control other risk factors and get screenings.

days.guide: Fill out the family health history together for parents, grandparents, siblings.

questions.q: Why share family health history with a doctor?
questions.a: It helps the doctor assess risk and recommend earlier screening or prevention.

days.guide: The child researches one disease and writes a prevention plan with 3 behaviors.

questions.q: Name two ways to lower type 2 diabetes risk.
questions.a: Regular physical activity (60 min/day for teens), balanced diet with fewer sugary drinks, healthy weight, enough sleep.

days.guide: The child presents to a family member.

questions.q: What does asthma do and how is it managed?
questions.a: It inflames and narrows airways; managed by avoiding triggers and using controller and quick-relief (rescue) inhalers as prescribed.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = defines the disease, explains causes and at least three risk factors (controllable vs. not), gives at least three prevention behaviors and cites 2 valid sources; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = facts without prevention plan; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Find three health product ads (acne cream, weight loss, sleep aid). Print a CRAAP checklist (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose). Have a brand-name and generic label (e.g., ibuprofen).
misconceptions: Thinking testimonials prove a product works. Correct: testimonials are individual stories, often paid; look for scientific evidence.
Believing generic medicine is weaker. Correct: FDA requires generics to have the same active ingredient, strength and effect as the brand.

days.guide: Analyze ads for testimonials, bandwagon, 'clinically proven' without citation, before/after photos.

questions.q: What's wrong with 'Doctors recommend!' with no details?
questions.a: It doesn't say which doctors or what evidence — an unsupported claim.

days.guide: Apply CRAAP to three health websites.

questions.q: What does 'Purpose' ask?
questions.a: Why the information exists — to inform, sell, persuade or entertain; sites selling products may be biased.

days.guide: Explain quackery signs (miracle cure, secret formula, works for many diseases, money-back pressure) and that the FTC fights deceptive advertising (FDA regulates labels/safety).

questions.q: What does the FTC do?
questions.a: The Federal Trade Commission protects consumers from false or deceptive advertising and fraud.

days.guide: Compare labels: same active ingredient (e.g., ibuprofen 200 mg), different price and inactive ingredients.

questions.q: A brand costs $9.99 for 100 tablets and generic $4.99 for 100. Same active ingredient — which is better value?
questions.a: The generic — same medicine at half the price ($0.05 vs. $0.10 per tablet).

days.guide: The child writes a consumer guide for one category (sunscreen, acne, protein bars): what to look for, red flags, trusted sources.

questions.q: What should you look for in sunscreen?
questions.a: Broad spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, water-resistant; reapply every 2 hours.

weeks.assessment_key: Consumer guide: 4 = clear criteria for choosing products, at least three red flags, compares cost/unit price, cites valid sources (FDA, AAD, NIH), practical tips; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = general opinions; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Bookmark CDC, CDPH and your county health department websites. Prepare a simple map and case list for an outbreak activity (e.g., John Snow's 1854 cholera map). Find career profiles (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook).
misconceptions: Thinking public health is only about hospitals. Correct: public health prevents disease in populations (vaccines, clean water, food inspections, tracking outbreaks).
Believing all health careers require medical school. Correct: many need a certificate, associate's or bachelor's degree.

days.guide: Compare roles: CDC (national), CDPH (state), county (local inspections, clinics, vaccines).

questions.q: Which agency inspects local restaurants?
questions.a: The county (or city) environmental health department.

days.guide: Plot cases on the map and find the cluster/source, like John Snow's Broad Street pump.

questions.q: What did John Snow discover in 1854?
questions.a: Mapping cholera deaths in London showed a cluster around the Broad Street water pump, showing cholera spread through contaminated water.

days.guide: Research two careers: duties, education, salary (BLS).

questions.q: What education does a registered nurse need?
questions.a: An associate's degree or bachelor's in nursing (ADN or BSN) and passing the NCLEX-RN licensing exam.

days.guide: Interview someone in a health job or watch a career video and take notes.

questions.q: What is one good interview question?
questions.a: Examples: 'What does a typical day look like?' 'What training did you need?' 'What's the hardest part?'

days.guide: The child makes a career profile card.

questions.q: What is an epidemiologist?
questions.a: A public health scientist who studies patterns and causes of disease in populations.

weeks.assessment_key: Career profile card: 4 = job title, duties, education/training, workplace, salary range (BLS), one interesting fact and personal connection; 3 = one element missing; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Prepare a campaign planning template (issue, data, audience, message, call to action, materials, timeline). Help locate valid sources.
misconceptions: Choosing a topic too broad ('health'). Correct: narrow to one behavior and audience ('getting 9 hours of sleep for middle schoolers').
Using opinions as evidence. Correct: cite data from valid sources.

days.guide: The child chooses a topic from the year and explains why it matters.

questions.q: Why is youth vaping a good advocacy topic?
questions.a: Example: many teens use or are exposed; nicotine is addictive and harms the developing brain; teens can influence peers.

days.guide: Gather three valid sources and two statistics.

questions.q: Give one valid source type.
questions.a: Government (.gov: CDC, CDPH), medical organizations (AAP, AHA), or university/hospital sites.

days.guide: Define audience and a specific call to action.

questions.q: Example call to action for a sleep campaign?
questions.a: 'Charge your phone outside your bedroom tonight.'

days.guide: Plan materials and timeline.

questions.q: Why match materials to audience?
questions.a: Different audiences use different media (video for teens, letter for officials).

days.guide: Share plan with a parent and revise.

questions.q: What makes advocacy different from just informing?
questions.a: Advocacy persuades people to take a specific healthy action or supports a change.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign plan: 4 = focused issue, 3 valid sources with data, defined audience, specific call to action, planned materials and timeline; 3 = one weak element; 2 = vague topic or no sources; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather art supplies or video tools. Prepare a short audience survey (before/after questions).
misconceptions: Thinking sharing once means success. Correct: measure impact with feedback or a survey.
Ignoring feedback. Correct: revise based on audience reactions.

days.guide: The child creates materials using the plan.

questions.q: Does your material include a clear message and call to action?
questions.a: Yes — check that both are visible and accurate.

days.guide: Revise with feedback.

questions.q: What feedback did you get and what did you change?
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer names specific changes (clearer wording, bigger visual).

days.guide: Share with audience.

questions.q: Who saw your campaign?
questions.a: Answers vary; should match the target audience.

days.guide: Survey the audience on knowledge and intent.

questions.q: How can a survey measure impact?
questions.a: Ask what they learned or whether they plan to change a behavior; compare before and after answers.

days.guide: Write reflection.

questions.q: What would you do differently?
questions.a: Answers vary; a good answer uses survey evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign and reflection: 4 = polished, accurate materials, shared with target audience, survey data reported, thoughtful reflection on impact and improvements; 3 = shared with some data; 2 = materials only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find the grade 7 wellness wheel (or draw one: physical, mental/emotional, social, safety, environmental, intellectual). Prepare a cumulative final (key below).
misconceptions: Making vague goals. Correct: use SMART goals with tracking.
Forgetting resources. Correct: list specific names and numbers (counselor, doctor, 988).

days.guide: Re-rate each wedge 1–10 and compare with grade 7.

questions.q: Which area improved most?
questions.a: Answers vary; the child should explain why.

days.guide: Write a high school wellness plan with SMART goals for physical, mental, social and safety health.

questions.q: Give one SMART physical goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will be active 60 minutes a day at least 5 days a week for the fall semester, tracked in a log.'

days.guide: List supports: counselor, doctor, family, coaches, 988.

questions.q: Name two high school resources.
questions.a: School counselor, school nurse, teachers/coaches, clubs, wellness center.

days.guide: Review key concepts from all units.

questions.q: What does Ask-Listen-Tell mean?
questions.a: Ask directly about suicide, listen without judgment, tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Give the final and share the plan.

questions.q: What reverses an opioid overdose?
questions.a: Naloxone.

weeks.assessment_key: Final key (sample): resilience definition; 988; protective factors; calcium 1,300 mg; supplements not FDA-approved before sale; abstinence 100%; consent clear/ongoing; minors 12+ STI consent; 0.01% under-21 BAC; naloxone; addiction = treatable disease; CPR 100–120/min; reach-throw-don't go; 5 D's; FTC false ads; CDC/CDPH roles. Wellness plan: 4 = SMART goals in four areas, supports, tracking plan.
